## The Condition

**Necessary and sufficient condition:** For every $j \in \{1,\ldots,m\}$ and every $\lambda = (\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_m) \in \mathbb{R}^m_+$ with $\sum_i \lambda_i = 1$ and $\sum_i \lambda_i u_i = u_j$, we have
$$y_j \;\leq\; \sum_{i=1}^m \lambda_i\, y_i. \tag{$\star$}$$

Equivalently, defining the **lower convex envelope**
$$h(x) \;=\; \min\Bigl\{\,\textstyle\sum_i \lambda_i\, y_i \;:\; \lambda \geq 0,\;\sum_i \lambda_i = 1,\;\sum_i \lambda_i u_i = x\Bigr\}, \qquad x \in P:=\operatorname{conv}\{u_1,\ldots,u_m\},$$
the condition is $h(u_j) = y_j$ for all $j$ (i.e., no data point lies strictly above the lower convex envelope of the data).

---

## Proof of Necessity

Suppose a convex $f:\mathbb{R}^k\to\mathbb{R}$ with $f(u_i)=y_i$ exists. Take any $j$ and any $\lambda\geq 0$, $\sum\lambda_i=1$, $\sum\lambda_i u_i = u_j$. By convexity of $f$:
$$y_j = f(u_j) = f\!\Bigl(\sum_i \lambda_i u_i\Bigr) \;\leq\; \sum_i \lambda_i\, f(u_i) = \sum_i \lambda_i\, y_i.$$
This is exactly $(\star)$. $\square$

---

## Proof of Sufficiency

Assume $(\star)$ holds. We construct a finite convex $f:\mathbb{R}^k\to\mathbb{R}$ with $f(u_i)=y_i$.

**Step 1: The lower convex envelope $h$ passes through every data point.**

The function $h$ is well-defined on the polytope $P = \operatorname{conv}\{u_i\}$ (the feasible set is nonempty for $x\in P$). Taking $\lambda_j=1$, $\lambda_i=0$ for $i\neq j$ gives $h(u_j) \leq y_j$. Condition $(\star)$ says that every feasible $\lambda$ with $\sum\lambda_i u_i = u_j$ satisfies $\sum\lambda_i y_i \geq y_j$, so $h(u_j) \geq y_j$. Hence
$$h(u_j) = y_j \quad\text{for all } j=1,\ldots,m. \tag{1}$$

**Step 2: $h$ is polyhedral convex on $P$.**

The epigraph of $h$ is:
$$\operatorname{epi}(h) = \bigl\{(x,t)\in P\times\mathbb{R} : \exists\,\lambda\geq 0,\;\sum\lambda_i=1,\;U\lambda=x,\;y^\top\lambda \leq t\bigr\},$$
where $U=[u_1|\cdots|u_m]\in\mathbb{R}^{k\times m}$. This is the projection of the polyhedron $\{(\lambda,x,t): \lambda\geq 0,\;\mathbf{1}^\top\lambda=1,\;U\lambda=x,\;y^\top\lambda\leq t\}$ onto the $(x,t)$-coordinates, hence is itself a polyhedron. Therefore $h$ is a **polyhedral convex function**: on $P$ it can be written as
$$h(x) = \max\{\ell_1(x),\;\ell_2(x),\;\ldots,\;\ell_N(x)\}, \qquad x\in P, \tag{2}$$
where each $\ell_j:\mathbb{R}^k\to\mathbb{R}$ is an affine function. (These correspond to the facets of $\operatorname{epi}(h)$; if $P$ is lower-dimensional, the affine functions on the affine span of $P$ extend to all of $\mathbb{R}^k$.)

**Step 3: Extension to all of $\mathbb{R}^k$.**

Define
$$f(x) \;=\; \max\{\ell_1(x),\;\ell_2(x),\;\ldots,\;\ell_N(x)\}, \qquad x\in\mathbb{R}^k.$$

- **Convexity:** $f$ is the pointwise maximum of finitely many affine (hence convex) functions, so $f$ is convex.
- **Finite everywhere ($\operatorname{dom}f = \mathbb{R}^k$):** Each $\ell_j$ is a real-valued affine function on $\mathbb{R}^k$, so $f(x) = \max_j \ell_j(x) < +\infty$ for every $x$, and $f(x) \geq \ell_1(x) > -\infty$.
- **Interpolation:** For each $u_i \in P$, by (2) we have $f(u_i) = h(u_i) = y_i$ by (1).

Therefore $f$ is a convex function with $\operatorname{dom}f = \mathbb{R}^k$ satisfying $f(u_i)=y_i$ for all $i=1,\ldots,m$. $\square$

---

## Summary

The necessary and sufficient condition is:

> **For every $j \in \{1,\ldots,m\}$ and every convex combination $\sum_i \lambda_i u_i = u_j$ (with $\lambda_i \geq 0$, $\sum_i \lambda_i = 1$), we have $y_j \leq \sum_i \lambda_i y_i$.**

This is the condition that each data point $(u_j, y_j)$ lies on (not strictly above) the lower convex envelope of the full dataset $\{(u_i,y_i)\}_{i=1}^m$ in $\mathbb{R}^{k+1}$.

- **Necessity** is immediate from the definition of convexity.
- **Sufficiency** follows by constructing the lower convex envelope $h$ on $P=\operatorname{conv}\{u_i\}$ (which equals $y_j$ at each $u_j$ by the condition), recognizing $h$ as polyhedral (its epigraph is a projected polyhedron), representing $h=\max\{\ell_1,\ldots,\ell_N\}$ as a maximum of affine functions on $P$, and extending this maximum to all of $\mathbb{R}^k$—yielding a finite convex function that interpolates the data.

This is exactly $(\star)$. $\square$

## Proof of Sufficiency

$$h(u_j) = y_j \quad\text{for all } j=1,\ldots,m. \tag{1}$$

The epigraph of $h$ is:
$$\operatorname{epi}(h) = \bigl\{(x,t)\in P\times\mathbb{R} : \exists\,\lambda\geq 0,\;\sum\lambda_i=1,\;U\lambda=x,\;y^\top\lambda \leq t\bigr\},$$
